beats.narration: Under these mounds of dirt in southeast Iowa, there are sixty-eight barrels.

claims.claim: 68 drums, more than 9,700 pounds, in earth-covered magazines.
claims.quote: approximately 68 drums, totaling more than 9,700 pounds net explosive weight, of stored lead azide inside earth-covered magazines
The drums are stored in two earth covered magazine (ECM) storage bunkers

beats.narration: Inside them is nearly five tons of an explosive so sensitive that, the Army says, slight friction or movement can set it off.

claims.quote: Nearly five tons of lead azide are set to be detonated

claims.claim: 68 drums, more than 9,700 pounds, in earth-covered magazines.
claims.quote: approximately 68 drums, totaling more than 9,700 pounds net explosive weight, of stored lead azide inside earth-covered magazines

claims.claim: Slight friction or movement can set it off.
claims.quote: making it vulnerable to accidental detonation from even slight friction or movement

beats.narration: It is the country's entire stockpile. And the Army says it cannot be moved.

claims.quote: plans to detonate the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning
It prevents those barrels from being able to be moved.

beats.narration: So the plan is to blow it up. Right where it sits. Wednesday morning, nine a.m.

claims.quote: controlled, in-place detonation of degraded, crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at approximately 9:00 a.m. CST

beats.narration: The dust from that blast will have lead in it.

claims.quote: a dust plume that will contain some lead

claims.quote: Local and federal officials strongly urge community members to vacate the evacuation area

claims.quote: told those up to 20 miles (32 kilometers) away to remain indoors with windows closed

claims.quote: wet-clean surfaces that may be contacted by infants or children, including outdoor play equipment, toys, tables and chairs
Areas of concern should be cleaned with a garden hose, wet rag, or baby wipe.

Safety Officer,

claims.claim: The liquid level has to be checked; the alcohol evaporates.
claims.quote: Periodic surveillance is then required both visually to assure adequate liquid level and testing to determine if ethanol evaporation has reduced antifreeze properties.

beats.say: How did we get here? This was not a surprise. In nineteen eighty-four, an Army safety officer wrote down exactly how this would go wrong.

claims.quote: leaving the stockpile of bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums
This March, inspectors looked at the 68 barrels.

beats.narration: Five tons of neglect.
onscreen: THE ARMY'S LEAD BOMB IN IOWA

claims.quote: Nearly five tons of lead azide are set to be detonated

beats.narration: To set off the main explosive in a shell or a bomb, you need a small, violent trigger first. A detonator.

claims.claim: Used in detonators to start other explosives.
claims.quote: It is used in detonators to initiate secondary explosives

claims.claim: A detonating agent for other explosives.
claims.quote: an explosive compound used as a detonating agent for other explosives

beats.narration: For about a hundred years, lead azide has been the stuff inside that trigger.

claims.quote: The U.S. started using lead azide 100 years ago to make munitions.

beats.say: For about a hundred years, led azide has been the stuff inside that trigger.

beats.narration: It goes off from heat, from a knock, from friction. That is the whole point of it.

claims.quote: It's very sensitive to heat, shock, and friction

beats.narration: A weapon only needs a tiny amount. A little cup of it, sealed inside the fuze.

claims.quote: miniature lead azide and lead styphnate cups inside their sealed fuzes

beats.narration: Now picture that little cup. Then picture sixty-eight barrels.

claims.claim: 68 drums, more than 9,700 pounds, in earth-covered magazines.
claims.quote: approximately 68 drums, totaling more than 9,700 pounds net explosive weight, of stored lead azide inside earth-covered magazines

beats.narration: And here is the strange part. The military stopped using it about fifteen years ago.
onscreen: THE MILITARY MOVED AWAY FROM IT ABOUT 15 YEARS AGO

claims.claim: The U.S. moved away from it about 15 years ago.
claims.quote: It moved away from the chemical about 15 years ago because of how hard it is to store and move.

beats.narration: So what is nearly five tons of it still doing in a bunker in Iowa?

claims.quote: Nearly five tons of lead azide are set to be detonated

beats.narration: The answer starts in that 1984 paper, written by the safety officer at an Army depot in Illinois.
onscreen: SAFETY OFFICER, SAVANNA ARMY DEPOT ACTIVITY

claims.quote: COMPLEXITIES OF LEAD AZIDE
Savanna Army Depot Activity
Savanna, Illinois

claims.claim: Presented to the DoD Explosives Safety Board's seminar.
claims.quote: DDESB Explosives Safety Seminar
29 August 1984

beats.say: The answer starts in that nineteen eighty-four paper, written by the safety officer at an Army depot in Illinois.

beats.narration: It says the war in Vietnam drove the development of weapons that used lead azide in, quote, relatively enormous quantities.
onscreen: Vietnam-era jungle warfare fostered the development of munitions using relatively enormous quantities of lead azide.

claims.quote: Vietnam-era jungle warfare fostered the development of munitions using relatively enormous quantities of lead azide.

beats.say: It says the war in Vietnam drove the development of weapons that used led azide in, quote, relatively enormous quantities.

beats.narration: But they were so sensitive that many of the people meant to use them did not want to.
onscreen: Their sensitivity to detonation caused a reluctance among many users to deploy them

claims.quote: Their sensitivity to detonation caused a reluctance among many users to deploy them, resulting in a stockpile of both munitions and bulk lead azide.

beats.narration: So when the war wound down, the military was left with a vast supply, and almost no demand.
onscreen: a vast supply and an extremely small demand

claims.quote: The winding down of hostilities left a vast supply and an extremely small demand.

beats.narration: They tried to sell it. Nobody bought it.
onscreen: Early attempts to sell the stockpiled lead azide were fruitless

claims.quote: Early attempts to sell the stockpiled lead azide were fruitless

beats.narration: So the Army started destroying it. And then it stopped. The paper says the project was halted with about half the stockpile gone.
onscreen: halted after approximately half the stockpile was destroyed

claims.claim: The Army's disposal project stopped about halfway.
claims.quote: The electrolysis project was halted after approximately half the stockpile was destroyed.

beats.narration: The other half stayed in drums. Drums that were already leaking. They were repacked, and the paper says that bought another ten to fifteen years.

claims.quote: The remaining drums in storage began leaking more frequently due to corrosion and were finally repacked, giving them another 10 to 15 years before they will need repacking again.

beats.narration: That was 1984.

claims.quote: 29 August 1984

beats.say: That was nineteen eighty-four.

beats.narration: Here is how you store this stuff. Dry, it is too sensitive to keep. So it is kept wet: in barrels, under liquid, inside concrete bunkers buried in earth.

claims.claim: Dry lead azide is too sensitive; it is stored under water.
claims.quote: its extreme sensitivity when dry necessitates under water storage
a reinforced structure made of concrete purpose-built to hold ammunition or explosives
in a bath of ethanol and water meant to keep it stable

beats.narration: And the same paper lists what can go wrong.

claims.quote: Long-term storage of lead azide presents some problems.

beats.narration: First. It has to stay under water.

claims.claim: Dry lead azide is too sensitive; it is stored under water.
claims.quote: its extreme sensitivity when dry necessitates under water storage

beats.narration: Second. If that water freezes, the paper says, it can go off on its own. So alcohol gets added, to keep it from freezing.

claims.quote: if the water freezes, spontaneous detonation occurs, presumably due to ice crystal formation breaking lead azide crystals
Addition of ethanol to the water is therefore necessary to make a non-freezing mixture.

beats.narration: Third. Alcohol evaporates. So somebody has to keep checking the level, and keep topping it up.
onscreen: SOMEONE HAS TO KEEP CHECKING THE LEVEL

claims.claim: The liquid level has to be checked; the alcohol evaporates.
claims.quote: Periodic surveillance is then required both visually to assure adequate liquid level and testing to determine if ethanol evaporation has reduced antifreeze properties.

beats.narration: And the containers do not last. In 1984 they were steel drums, and the paper says steel rusts through.

claims.quote: the steel 55-gallon packing and storage drum has a limited life due to rust-through, which eventually results in leakage of the ethanol-water mix
29 August 1984

beats.say: And the containers do not last. In nineteen eighty-four they were steel drums, and the paper says steel rusts through.

beats.narration: So this is a material that is only safe for as long as somebody keeps looking after it.
So let's count the chances there were to deal with it.
1984. The risks are on paper, and half the stockpile is still in drums.

claims.quote: 29 August 1984

claims.claim: The Army's disposal project stopped about halfway.
claims.quote: The electrolysis project was halted after approximately half the stockpile was destroyed.

beats.say: nineteen eighty-four. The risks are on paper, and half the stockpile is still in drums.

beats.narration: In 2004, a Defense Department assessment raises concern about an old stockpile of lead azide that has been deteriorating for forty years.

claims.quote: An environmental assessment from 2004 shows the Department of Defense was concerned about an old stockpile of lead azide that had been deteriorating for 40 years at the plant in Middletown.

beats.say: In 2004, a Defense Department assessment raises concern about an old stockpile of led azide that has been deteriorating for forty years.

beats.narration: 2009. The Army gathers up what is left of the country's lead azide and moves it to one place: the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in Middletown. Some of it is already more than sixty years old. It goes into new plastic barrels.
onscreen: THE WHOLE STOCKPILE MOVES TO IOWA

claims.quote: (about 10,000 pounds, some already 60+ years old) was consolidated from various bases during base realignment and moved to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAP)
transferred from metal barrels to plastic barrels
The Army moved all of the country’s lead azide to Middletown in 2009.

beats.say: 2009. The Army gathers up what is left of the country's led azide and moves it to one place: the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in Middletown. Some of it is already more than sixty years old. It goes into new plastic barrels.

beats.narration: Around 2011, the military stops using lead azide altogether.

claims.quote: 2011 or earlier: U.S. military moved away from procuring/using lead azide because of sensitivity and storage/handling challenges.

beats.say: Around 2011, the military stops using led azide altogether.

beats.narration: The routine: an inspection every month, and a top-up of the liquid every September, before winter.

claims.quote: Routine schedule: Drums were inspected monthly; annual inspections and water/ethanol refilling occurred in September prior to winter freezing temps.

beats.narration: September 2025. According to the government's own court filing, that is the last time the liquid was checked and refilled.
onscreen: GOVERNMENT COURT BRIEF, AS REPORTED BY IOWA PUBLIC RADIO

claims.claim: A government court brief: the liquid went unchecked and unreplenished from September 2025.
claims.quote: The government’s brief in support of this week’s detonation says the water-ethanol mixture used to keep the explosive stable had gone unchecked and unreplenished since September 2025.

beats.say: September twenty twenty-five. According to the government's own court filing, that is the last time the liquid was checked and refilled.

beats.narration: That same month, the plant's contractor asks an outside firm for a price to get rid of the barrels.
onscreen: PLANT CONTRACTOR ASKS FOR A DISPOSAL QUOTE

claims.quote: American Ordnance, the plant contractor that operates the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, asked MuniRem for a disposal quote on Sept. 24, 2025, according to documents and a timeline shared with IPR by the company.

beats.narration: March 11, 2026. An inspection finds the lead azide has crystallized. The next day the Army tells the EPA, and the plant shuts down for eighteen days.

claims.quote: A routine monitoring inspection on March 11, 2026, found that decades-old, stored lead azide had partially crystallized

claims.claim: EPA was told the next day.
claims.quote: 3/12/2026 -- EPA Region 7 was notified of 68 drums of potentially unstable lead (Pb) azide
since the plant closed for an 18-day emergency safety review in March

beats.say: March eleventh, twenty twenty-six. An inspection finds the led azide has crystallized. The next day the Army tells the E.P.A., and the plant shuts down for eighteen days.

beats.narration: And the plant's commander tells the public, quote: there is no immediate danger to the public.
onscreen: "There is no immediate danger to the public."

claims.quote: There is no immediate danger to the public.

beats.narration: Within two weeks, the Army hires a company to treat the barrels chemically. No blast, no dust cloud. By May, that is dropped, and the Secretary of the Army has chosen detonation.
onscreen: MARCH: A CONTRACT TO TREAT IT CHEMICALLY

claims.quote: Within two weeks of that March warning, the Army hired MuniRem Environmental after a panel recommended chemical neutralization. But by May 8, the secretary of the Army had chosen to blow up the drums where they stood

claims.claim: Chemical treatment would avoid the dust.
claims.quote: Chemical neutralization would avoid the plume of dust
On May 14, the Army told MuniRem it would not exercise the treatment portion of its contract.

beats.narration: October 15. The Army holds an open house in Middletown. One of Iowa's own senators says those talks left out how far the lead dust could travel.
onscreen: LEFT OUT: HOW FAR THE DUST COULD TRAVEL

claims.quote: 10/15/2026 -- The Army held an Open House with nearly 200 residents and community leaders
Ernst said the Army began discussing disposal with some communities months ago, but those discussions left out how far dust containing lead could travel.

beats.say: October fifteenth. The Army holds an open house in Middletown. One of Iowa's own senators says those talks left out how far the led dust could travel.

beats.narration: November 13. The EPA grants the permit to blow it up.

claims.quote: EPA issued an emergency permit that became effective on November 13, 2026

beats.say: November thirteenth. The E.P.A. grants the permit to blow it up.

beats.narration: November 15. The Army announces the date, five days out, and publishes the maps. The dust cloud on those maps reaches about 100 miles.

claims.claim: The public notice came five days ahead.
claims.quote: 11/15/2026 -- Army issued its 5-day advance public notification
a plume of dust containing lead particles that could extend as far as 100 miles away

beats.say: November fifteenth. The Army announces the date, five days out, and publishes the maps. The dust cloud on those maps reaches about 100 miles.

beats.narration: The next day, the governor's office says, is when it learned of the plan. From that public advisory.
onscreen: GOVERNOR'S OFFICE: LEARNED FROM THE PUBLIC ADVISORY

claims.claim: A spokesperson for Gov. Reynolds. The advisory was issued Sunday, Nov. 15.
claims.quote: The Office of the Governor became aware of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant's plan to detonate degraded lead azide on Monday after a public advisory was issued by the U.S. Army

beats.narration: The blast is set for November 20. Then November 23. Then, after a lawsuit and a post from the President, November 25.

claims.quote: That was the second time it was publicly delayed, after being scheduled for Nov. 20 and Nov. 23.
on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at approximately 9:00 a.m. CST
Iowa environmental groups file a petition for review against the EPA, challenging the permit authorizing the detonation
President Donald Trump says he has ordered the military to hold off on the planned detonation until the federal appeals court and Sand, the incoming Iowa governor, sign off on it.
The appeals court denies the environmental group's emergency motion and lifts the administrative stay on the permit, clearing the way for the detonation.

beats.say: The blast is set for November twentieth. Then November twenty-third. Then, after a lawsuit and a post from the President, November twenty-fifth.

beats.narration: Look at that whole line. The warning was written in 1984. The public got the date, and the map, five days ahead.

claims.quote: 29 August 1984

claims.claim: The public notice came five days ahead.
claims.quote: 11/15/2026 -- Army issued its 5-day advance public notification

beats.say: Look at that whole line. The warning was written in nineteen eighty-four. The public got the date, and the map, five days ahead.

beats.narration: One of Iowa's Republican senators said it plainly. These materials should never have been allowed to get to this point.
onscreen: "These materials should never have been allowed to get to this point."

claims.quote: These materials should never have been allowed to get to this point, and Iowans are right to be frustrated.

beats.narration: For decades, the answer was later. Later showed up.
So what happened inside those barrels? The liquid went down.

claims.quote: The ethanol-water bath the lead azide sits in had evaporated, and the explosive had re-crystallized.

beats.narration: When lead azide dries out, it grows crystals. Long, needle-shaped ones.

claims.quote: Pure lead azide occurs as colorless needle-like crystals.
inspectors identified severe material degradation and crystallization

beats.say: When led azide dries out, it grows crystals. Long, needle-shaped ones.

beats.narration: And the 1984 paper says it in one line. Breaking these crystals is believed to initiate detonation.
onscreen: Breaking these crystals is believed to initiate detonation.

claims.quote: Breaking these crystals is believed to initiate detonation.
29 August 1984

beats.say: And the nineteen eighty-four paper says it in one line. Breaking these crystals is believed to initiate detonation.

beats.narration: By this fall, the Army says, crystals had built up on the outside of the barrels. On the lids. On the bolts.

claims.quote: We've observed a significant accumulation of crystallized lead azide on the exterior of the barrels, including the barrel lids.
because of the crystallization on each of the bolts on the view ports and on the lids

beats.narration: So nobody can open a lid to add liquid. The head of the ATF said just removing one lid could set off that barrel, and then every other barrel in the bunker.

claims.quote: just removing the lid from one of those containers could cause a detonation of that barrel and the sympathetic detonation of each and every barrel inside either one of those magazines

beats.say: So nobody can open a lid to add liquid. The head of the A.T.F. said just removing one lid could set off that barrel, and then every other barrel in the bunker.

beats.narration: They cannot be moved. They cannot be trucked somewhere safer.

claims.quote: It prevents those barrels from being able to be moved.
unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of an uncontrolled detonation

beats.narration: And winter is coming. Less liquid means what is left freezes more easily. Freezing is the exact thing the 1984 paper warned about.

claims.claim: Col. Teller, in a court filing.
claims.quote: less liquid inside the barrels means the solution is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the risk of an explosive chain reaction
if the water freezes, spontaneous detonation occurs, presumably due to ice crystal formation breaking lead azide crystals
29 August 1984

beats.say: And winter is coming. Less liquid means what is left freezes more easily. Freezing is the exact thing the nineteen eighty-four paper warned about.

beats.narration: An engineer who filed a statement for the groups suing over the permit said: stored properly, it should not deteriorate. It only happens when storage is not carefully monitored.
onscreen: "It's only when the conditions of storage are not carefully monitored that it starts to form crystals"

claims.quote: Ordinarily, if you store it properly, it should not deteriorate. It should stay for a long long time. It’s only when the conditions of storage are not carefully monitored that it starts to form crystals and things of that sort.
Dr. Ron Sahu, a combustion expert and environmental engineer, wrote to the court to supplement environmental groups’ lawsuit against the EPA.

beats.narration: So here is the plan. Two rapid detonations, inside the bunkers.

claims.quote: two consecutive, rapid detonations
The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines

beats.narration: Around them: walls of sand-filled barriers two stories high. Water tanks. Foam. Gel blocks. And misters soaking the ground and the air.

claims.quote: sand-filled HESCO barriers standing about two stories high
aqueous foam blocks, two walls of four 16,000-gallon water tanks, and gel blocks adjacent to the bunkers
High-volume industrial misting units and water sprayers will thoroughly saturate the soil and airspace before and during detonation

beats.narration: The Army says its goal is to keep as much of the dust as it can on its own property.
onscreen: GOAL: KEEP IT ON THE PLANT

claims.quote: Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling.

beats.narration: And the Army's argument is simple. Leave it, and it goes off on its own. No warning. No barriers. Nobody evacuated.

claims.quote: is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance
It's just a matter of time when we have an uncontrolled detonation.

beats.narration: The general in charge said: inaction is no longer an option.
onscreen: MAJ. GEN. ERIC SHIRLEY, U.S. ARMY SUSTAINMENT COMMAND

claims.quote: "Inaction is no longer an option," said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general, U.S. Army Sustainment Command.

beats.narration: A federal appeals court agreed. So did Iowa's governor. So did the mayor of Middletown.

claims.quote: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily put the Environmental Protection Agency’s permit on hold last week
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said Tuesday she supports the U.S. Army’s plan to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead azide
Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place "so we can move on with our lives."

beats.narration: And today? They are probably right.
But it is only true today. Because of everything that did not happen before today.
It could have been destroyed while it was stable. The Army was already doing that when the 1984 paper was written. It stopped halfway.
onscreen: DESTROY IT WHILE IT IS STABLE

claims.claim: The Army's disposal project stopped about halfway.
claims.quote: The electrolysis project was halted after approximately half the stockpile was destroyed.
29 August 1984

beats.say: It could have been destroyed while it was stable. The Army was already doing that when the nineteen eighty-four paper was written. It stopped halfway.

beats.narration: The Army's own spokesperson calls Middletown an anomaly. Everywhere else, she says, stockpiles like this were eliminated over the last two decades.

claims.quote: According to Army spokesperson Justine Barati, the stockpile in Middletown is an anomaly.
over the past two decades, the Department of Defense has "systematically conducted demilitarization campaigns to eliminate bulk legacy stores across the industrial base."

beats.narration: It could have been kept wet. That was the whole job.

claims.claim: A government court brief: the liquid went unchecked and unreplenished from September 2025.
claims.quote: The government’s brief in support of this week’s detonation says the water-ethanol mixture used to keep the explosive stable had gone unchecked and unreplenished since September 2025.

claims.claim: The liquid level has to be checked; the alcohol evaporates.
claims.quote: Periodic surveillance is then required both visually to assure adequate liquid level and testing to determine if ethanol evaporation has reduced antifreeze properties.

beats.narration: And it could have been treated this spring. By the contractor's account, a review panel recommended exactly that, and the Army hired the contractor to do it.

claims.quote: According to a timeline provided by MuniRem, a panel that included Army specialists, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory personnel and EPA representatives voted March 19 to recommend chemical neutralization as the safest treatment.
The Army awarded MuniRem a contract March 25

beats.narration: The Army says crystals around the lids made opening the barrels too dangerous. What changed between March and May has not been made public.

claims.quote: the Army said crystals may have migrated into the drums’ lid assemblies, where friction from opening them could cause an explosion

claims.claim: What the records do not show.
claims.quote: They leave unanswered what changed between the March recommendation and the May decision

beats.narration: The window to do this safely was open for decades. It closed because nobody went through it.
So where does the dust go? Wherever the wind is going that morning.

claims.quote: said the direction the wind blows will determine where the plume reaches

beats.narration: The first maps, for the first date, sent the cloud northeast. About 100 miles.

claims.quote: the blast zone appears to stretch approximately 100 miles northeast from the blast site

claims.claim: Snopes checked it against the Army's maps.
claims.quote: We compared this map to maps the Army released ahead of the planned detonations and found they aligned.

beats.narration: Up the Mississippi, and over it, into Illinois. The Illinois environmental agency said nobody had notified it.

claims.quote: The Army's maps modeling where the plume could reach include parts of Illinois
officials from Illinois' EPA said they had not been notified about the detonation

beats.narration: In Mediapolis, less than twenty miles from the plant, city officials learned where they stood when the first map put them in the middle of it.

claims.quote: In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure on Sunday, when the initial map put them in the center of the dust exposure area.

beats.say: In Meedy-apolis, less than twenty miles from the plant, city officials learned where they stood when the first map put them in the middle of it.

beats.narration: Then the date moved. And the wind turned around.

claims.quote: The wind was out of the southeast on Friday, which would have pushed the plume north if the detonations happened that day.
The wind flipped and was expected to come out of the northwest on Monday.

beats.narration: The newest maps send the cloud the other way. Southwest, across the corner of Iowa, and into northeast Missouri.

claims.quote: show a plume of toxic dust drifting southwest toward northeast Missouri
By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City.
it narrows to a band running from the Burlington and Keokuk area toward Macon, Missouri, with Quincy, Illinois, just southeast of it

beats.narration: A University of Iowa professor put it like this. People who were worried a few days ago are off the hook. People who thought they would be fine are now right in the path.
onscreen: "...those who thought they were going to be OK are now right in the plume path."

claims.quote: So folks that were very concerned even several days ago now are in a sense off the hook, and those who thought they were going to be OK are now right in the plume path,
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa

beats.narration: Same blast. Different people downwind. Decided by the weather on a Wednesday morning.
And remember what these maps are. They are forecasts. How they were built has not been made public. That same professor called them a guesstimate.
onscreen: "It is a guesstimate at this point"

claims.quote: The maps are forecasts and will change with the weather.
